card.title: Short Story 7 — An Astrologer's Day (R. K. Narayan)

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: ## The story at a glance "An Astrologer's Day" by R. K. Narayan is a story about a man who tells fortunes he does not believe in — and whose one true prophecy arrives by accident. The astrologer works under a tamarind tree in a crowded market, wrapped in a turban and sacred marks, reading faces with the cunning of long practice.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
The astrologer once left the man for dead — his guess is actually knowledge, not magic.
Irony: he earns a living by 'reading stars' but cannot read his own past; guilt resolved at dusk.

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Trick 3: Atmosphere questions: the twilight crowd, the flare, the market — sensory detail hides his ordinary trickery; link setting to theme of deception.  ·  ## The characters worth an essay **The astrologer** is Narayan's great ordinary man: shrewd, fraudulent, tired, and secretly guilty. The sketch the exam wants has three layers — the professional (the costume and the patter), the private man (a village past, a wife, a child, a debt), and the buried criminal (a knife, a well, twelve years of weight).…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: ## The themes worth an essay **Irony of fate** — the theme and the plot are the same thing here: chance arranges the meeting, the recognition and the release, and no character plans any of it. **Guilt and its unburdening** — twelve years of carried blood lifted in one evening; the story argues that confession, even partial, is survival.…  ·  ## How NEB asks it **"Why did the astrologer leave his village?" (4 marks)** — the quarrel, the knife, the well, the flight; told in his confession to the wife. **"What did the astrologer tell Guru Nayak, and why?"** — the false prophecy as self-protection and as mercy; name both motives.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Q. How does the astrologer know so much about Guru Nayak? (2 marks) — he was the village youth who stabbed him and left him for dead.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## The plot, retold with an eye on its turns The setup is a portrait of professional bluff: the astrologer's equipment (cowrie shells, charts, a shawl that looks holy), his client-reading technique — "he knew what he would say" only after studying the face — and his honest inner admission: he had "a working analysis of mankind's troubles", not a knowledge of stars.…  ·  ## The devices, with evidence - **Irony of fate** — the master device, stacked: a fake astrologer makes one true prophecy; the truth is his own crime; the client hunting his attacker is brought to him by chance; and the "prophecy" that ends the hunt is a lie told for self-protection that also, genuinely, saves both men.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: The astrologer's power is KNOWLEDGE, not the stars — he knows Guru Nayak because he left him for dead years ago; this twist is the whole story.  ·  Trick 2: Irony and fate: the man he 'killed' survived and searched for him — the astrologer is both the criminal and the comforter; state the double role.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q. Why does the astrologer feel relieved at the end? (2 marks) — the man he thought he murdered is alive; his lifelong guilt lifts.
